p: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.

notes: The article lists the fourth occupation as 'craftsmen/merchants'; I wrote merchants.
The article names seven clans; I gave two.
The article credits Wu Zetian with establishing the metropolitan examination and the jinshi/juren degrees; kept as it says, though simplified to jinshi.
